summary: A 1974 note on how the facilities used for TIP and TENEX accounting could be reused for collecting data from many sites across the network, beyond accounting alone. It explores the wider usefulness of those protocols.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 672 describes a way for a TIP to send accounting data to several possible servers while choosing only one to record it. The design avoids duplicate entries but accepts a risk of losing data if a collector fails at the wrong time.

questions: how did tip accounting data reach servers
subtitle: A protocol for sending data to multiple possible collectors without recording it twice.

tldr.problem: Sending a data request to more than one collector can prevent data loss but risks duplicate records, while sending it to one collector risks losing data if that collector fails.
tldr.mechanism: Collectors temporarily hold a request and echo it to the generator; the generator tells one collector to keep the data and tells the others to discard it.
tldr.outcome: The described TIP-TENEX accounting system was partially operational on selected hosts. Its policy avoids duplicate entries at the cost of possible data loss in some failure windows.

today: The unit records RFC 672's status as Unknown and lists no updates or obsoleting RFCs. It describes a multi-site data collection protocol applied to TIP-TENEX accounting.

sections.title: The Risk of Losing or Duplicating Data
sections.content:
The RFC discusses a data generator sending information to a service provided by collector processes at multiple network sites. Simply sending a request to one server and trying another after a timeout can create duplicate records if the first reply was delayed, or data loss if a request to one server is not processed.

The document presents protocols for a multi-site data collection facility and then applies them to TIP accounting, where TENEX hosts run accounting server processes. The memo says the system was partially operational on selected hosts for about a month.
sections.plainLanguage: If a sender cannot tell whether a server received a request, trying another server may either save the data or record it twice. The protocol delays permanent recording until one collector is selected.

sections.title: Acknowledge, Select and Discard
sections.content:
A TIP sends a data message to one, some or all accounting servers. A server willing to handle it buffers the message and returns the message to the TIP as an “I've got it” reply. The TIP sends “go ahead” to the first acceptable reply and sends “discard” to other servers that replied.

The selected server appends the relevant data to its accounting file after the go-ahead. The TIP then reduces its local counters by the data returned from the selected server. A sequence number lets the TIP distinguish replies to the current group of requests from late replies to earlier requests.
sections.plainLanguage: Servers hold the data temporarily and return it to the TIP. The TIP chooses one server to save it and tells other servers that replied to discard their copies.

sections.title: Retries and Duplicate Protection
sections.content:
If no server replies, the TIP accumulates new accounting data and sends another request. A later request can cancel data an accounting server has buffered but not yet received permission to record, subject to the same-sequence-number rule described in the RFC. A server that cannot accept data can remain silent, and the TIP may try it again.

The report says retransmission is the normal response to lost or garbled requests and replies. Its initial implementation sends accumulated data about every half hour, then tries about every five minutes until it succeeds. It remembers a favored server to try first and can send to all servers if that server does not respond quickly.
sections.plainLanguage: The TIP retries when it does not get a reply and uses sequence numbers to reject old replies. It normally tries its favored server first, then can contact all servers.

sections.title: The Reliability Trade-Off
sections.content:
The protocol is designed to avoid duplicate accounting entries, even though this can allow data loss in some cases. For example, if a collector receives “go ahead” but crashes before completing the file update, the data may be lost. The authors identify other loss cases, including prolonged unavailability of collectors until TIP counters overflow.

The RFC says the design can be adjusted for applications that prefer avoiding loss at the cost of possible duplicates. It is suited to data that is independent or commutative, such as counts, and may need more buffering for other kinds of data.
sections.plainLanguage: The design favors avoiding duplicate records, but it cannot prevent every loss. Other applications could change the trade-off and use more storage to protect different kinds of data.
